Threat.value: I jump or startle at ordinary sounds that would not bother most people
I listen for sounds that might mean someone is entering my home
I feel on guard even inside my own home

I have lost my faith in people, life, or a higher power
I was betrayed by someone I trusted

vignette: He was thirty-two, a European-American combat pilot whose flight hours on the F-35 had been marked by discipline and precision. During a November 2022 night briefing at the base armory, a junior squadron member approached him with a grin and a whispered request for a favor. The conversation abruptly turned when the officer forced him into a dim storage room, and a hand closed around his neck. The assault left him feeling betrayed and with a sudden loss of faith in people who were supposed to protect him. He reports that whenever people act suspiciously-a glance, a pause, an off-hand remark-his heart pounds and he flinches at ordinary sounds like a radio chatter or a distant aircraft roar. These perceived threats spark a fire of fear: the first step of his threat response is a startle to sounds that would normally go unnoticed by others. The noise of a fellow pilot's call sign in the cockpit or a sudden alarm on the flight deck instantly brings him to a state of high alert, and he feels a surge of terror that makes him instinctively think of potential danger. His appraisal of the incident hardened into a belief that he is a bad cop, that he cannot protect himself or others, and that he has been betrayed by someone he once trusted. These negative appraisals magnify every sensation of threat, because he interprets even a routine check of flight instruments as an opportunity for a second assault. The conviction that he is a failure fuels a heightened state of vigilance: he hears the wind over the wing and thinks it could be a hostile aircraft, and the hum of the avionics makes him feel watched. The belief that he betrayed himself and lost faith in others does not just feed his sense of danger; it also feeds a hyper-suspicious view of the environment. He now sees people acting suspiciously in the control room, in the mess hall, even when a co-pilot simply asks for a coffee. The feeling that he has been betrayed by a trusted squad member turns everyday gestures into potential threats, and each suspicious action he perceives becomes a trigger that keeps him on edge. His constant alert at home-he checks every window, listens for any sound that could be an intruder-reinforces the idea that he is unfit to survive. The startle responses to normal sounds reinforce his belief that he is a bad cop, that he has failed in his duty, and that his faith is lost. Each moment of intrusive monitoring in the dark of night, when he hears his own breathing, seems like a reminder that he is alone and vulnerable, and he concludes that he cannot trust himself or anyone else. Because the threat response is so intense, it colors his perception of the world. When a fellow pilot's face is partially shadowed by the flight deck lighting, his sense of threat triggers an automatic suspicion. Even the sound of a maintenance crew moving supplies triggers a flash of the assault: the memory of that sudden, cold hand that had slipped onto him. The more he is on guard, the more he interprets ordinary interactions as signs of danger, creating a self-reinforcing loop that tightens with every alarm. Over the past year he has lost sleep, withdrawn from flight simulations, and his performance has dipped. The constant mental check for danger has made him doubt his own competence, leading to a fear of making a mistake in a real combat mission. It was a routine check of his navigation system one night that finally pushed him to seek help, because he realized that his fear was costing him his career and his ability to protect the very people he vowed to serve. He hopes therapy can untangle the tangled loop of suspicion, threat, and self-criticism, and that he can rebuild trust in himself and others.
